objective: Start with the shared parts Plant, animal and bacterial cells all have cytoplasm and a cell membrane. Plant and animal cells are eukaryotic: their genetic material is enclosed in a nucleus. These are typical cell models; particular specialised cells can differ from the familiar diagram.

objective: Locate bacterial DNA Bacteria are prokaryotic and much smaller than typical plant or animal cells. They have cytoplasm, a cell membrane and a surrounding cell wall. Their genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus: the main DNA is a single circular loop in the cytoplasm. Bacteria also have ribosomes; no nucleus does not mean no genetic material.

objective: Recognise plasmids A bacterium may also contain one or more plasmids: small rings of DNA separate from its main DNA loop. Plasmids carry genes that can provide useful features, for example resistance to an antibiotic. They are not tiny nuclei, and not every bacterial cell has them. A bacterial cell wall should not be confused with the cellulose wall of a plant cell.

objective: Compare scale, not drawing size The model diagrams are symbolic and are not drawn to a common scale. Use supplied measurements to compare cells. objective: Control and chemical reactions Most animal cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes. The nucleus contains genetic material that controls cell activities. Cytoplasm is where most of the cell’s chemical reactions take place, with enzymes helping reactions. The cell membrane controls movement of substances into and out of the cell; it is not the same structure as a cell wall.

objective: Release energy and build proteins Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which transfers energy for cell processes. Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis. Plant cells also have mitochondria and ribosomes: photosynthesis does not remove the need for respiration. Small dots in our model represent ribosomes symbolically, not their appearance under an ordinary school light microscope.

objective: Recognise plant structures Plant and algal cells have a cellulose cell wall that strengthens the cell. Many plant cells have a permanent vacuole filled with cell sap; pressure from its contents helps support the cell. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis. Not every plant cell contains chloroplasts: root cells and onion-bulb epidermal cells are useful counterexamples. A cell wall and other structural evidence can support plant identification even without chloroplasts.

objective: Use evidence and sensible estimates Recognise structures using position, boundaries and supplied labels, not colour alone. Models simplify shape, number and relative scale. Estimate a structure’s size when an exact edge or measurement is uncertain; state the assumption rather than pretend an estimate is exact. objective: Enlargement is not detail Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the real object. Resolution is the ability to distinguish two nearby points as separate. Enlarging a blurred image does not recover missing detail. Electron microscopes have higher magnification and resolving power than light microscopes, allowing finer sub-cellular structures to be studied and increasing biological understanding as microscopy developed.

objective: Keep the units consistent Magnification = image size ÷ real size. Rearrange: real size = image size ÷ magnification; image size = magnification × real size. Convert units before dividing:1 mm =1000 μm,1 μm =1000 nm. A10 mm image of a20 μm cell has magnification10,000÷20=500. Magnification is a ratio with no length unit. A20 μm scale bar describes real length; its drawn length changes if an image is resized.
